You can build your vocabulary by paying attention to special words which may have different meanings depending on how they are used.
Hold on just a second … I'm paying for my java.

When you learn new words, sometimes one word will have different meanings (even with the same spelling). These words are called homographs.
Some homographs have the same spelling and pronunciation but different meanings. These are called homonyms.

Some homographs include:
ball → round object, dance
bear → animal, tolerate
box → container, fight
can → container, able to
colon → body part, punctuation
date → something on the calendar, appointment, fruit
fan → someone who admires something, something to keep a room cool
gum → part of mouth, something to chew
mole → animal, spot on one's body
ring → circle, call, sound of a bell
Look at the examples of homographs from the text:
Did you talk to Amy a second time?
The staff person who needed the weekend off had to change her plans.
You just need to bring change for the parking meter.
I don't have to close the restaurant on Friday.
We can use my car to carry all the heavy cans.
You sometimes pronounce words differently in speaking because of assimilation.
Did you talk to Amy a second time?

Assimilation refers to when two sounds come together to make a new sound. You do this when you are speaking and the words link to each other in your sentences; thus, reducing the sounds. The pronunciation that results is different from the individual sounds of the words when said separately.

Would you like some coffee?
Why don't you eat meat?
Come and kiss your mother.

Would you like some coffee? →/wouldja like some coffee/
Why don't you eat meat? →/why doncha eat meat/
Come and kiss your mother. →/come and kissyur mother/

images.text:
Peter: Hello? Hold on just a second … I'm paying for my java … Okay, hi Vanessa.
Vanessa: Hi Peter. Did you talk to Amy a second time? Does she still want to give you a hand with your cleanse and preparing your meals?
Peter : Yeah, she does. She's coming by this weekend to look at the recipes and the cookbook and make a shopping list. We might still need your help with some of the recipes. Will you be able to take a call while you're at work?
Vanessa: I have an even better idea. The staff person who needed the weekend off had to change her plans, so I'm free for the whole weekend and I don't have to close the restaurant on Friday.
Peter: Wow, that's great! You can relax and not think about cooking, except for when we call you for advice.

Vanessa: Well, what do you think about this idea? I will teach you and Amy to cook this weekend. Amy's close to me, and I know she's got a great kitchen with all the equipment and tools we need. We can spend the weekend at her place cooking together. I haven't been able to spend much time with either of you, so we can take this time to catch up and also get you some new and improved eating habits. Also, we can use my car to carry all the heavy cans. You just need to bring change for the parking meter so I don't get a fine.

Peter: Are you sure? That would be great. Wait, what cans?
Vanessa: Beans, Peter. You're going to be getting your protein from beans. You can't have meat or dairy, remember?
Peter: Oh right. Hmmm. Maybe I shouldn't have asked Amy to help me.
Vanessa: It will be fine. I'm stoked! This is going to be a blast. And after a few days, I promise you won't miss your coffee. Quitting will be a piece of cake.
Peter: I'll believe it when I see it. I really appreciate your help Vanessa.
